answer: Memory-hard minting resists sybils: creating each identity requires evaluating a function that needs gigabytes of fast RAM held for the whole computation, and that memory cannot be time-shared across concurrent evals. An ocean of k fakes minted in parallel demands k times the RAM at once — a mesa of memory no commodity box holds — so a farm is bound by aggregate memory, the costliest resource to scale. Running them serially instead trades money for a slow tide of sequential delay. Precondition: the function is genuinely memory-hard, so cost cannot be amortized across identities.
